title: Imran Khan Leave-India Notice Puts OCI Rights and Limits in Focus
excerpt: The US citizen and OCI cardholder must leave by October 28 after a Mumbai protest — a case that clarifies what an OCI card protects and what it does not.
body:
• Actor Imran Khan, a US citizen and OCI cardholder, has been told by Mumbai Police to leave India by October 28 after joining an October 10 protest in Mumbai.
  • An OCI card is not Indian citizenship: it gives a lifelong multiple-entry visa and parity with NRIs in some areas, but no vote and no right to contest elections.
  • The notice cites Sections 7 and 29 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, which let the Centre regulate a foreign national's presence and direct removal.
  • For OCI holders: the Article 19 right to assemble belongs to citizens, so protests carry immigration risk even though Articles 14 and 21 protect every person.

Mumbai Police have issued a Leave India Notice to actor Imran Khan, directing the US citizen and Overseas Citizen of India cardholder to leave the country by October 28. The action follows his participation on October 10 in a protest at August Kranti Maidan demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

Khan, 43, the nephew of Aamir Khan, was among about 400 people detained at the demonstration linked to the Cockroach Janta Party, and was released later. A complaint by former BJP MP Kirit Somaiya, who questioned whether a foreign national could join a political agitation, was forwarded for examination before the notice was served following action by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office.

What an OCI card does — and does not do

The distinction at the centre of this case is often misunderstood in the diaspora. As the explainer in The Times of India sets out, an OCI card, introduced in 2005 for people of Indian origin holding foreign citizenship, does not confer Indian citizenship. Holders remain foreign nationals in Indian law.

What the card does provide is substantial: a lifelong, multiple-entry visa, and specified benefits on travel, work, education and property, broadly on parity with non-resident Indians and subject to applicable rules. What it does not provide is political membership. OCI holders cannot vote or contest Parliament or state legislature elections, and their status gives no unconditional right to remain in India.

The powers invoked against Khan

Both reports cite the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. Section 7 empowers the Central Government to regulate, restrict or prohibit the entry, departure, presence or movement of foreigners, and to impose conditions on their stay. Section 29 provides for removal of a foreigner for contravention of the Act, its rules or orders, or on an adverse security report.

Police officials said foreign nationals are barred from joining political protests or activities on Indian soil. The notice is an administrative immigration measure. As LawBeat notes in its account, its issuance is not by itself a criminal conviction or a court finding that an offence was committed, and further administrative procedures are under way.

Can OCI holders join a protest?

Legal commentary in the Times of India explainer draws a careful line. Supreme Court advocate Amitraj Kaushal said no provision expressly bars an OCI holder from joining a peaceful gathering. The problem is the source of the right itself: freedom to assemble peacefully under Article 19 is a citizens' right, and an OCI holder cannot invoke it on the same basis as a citizen. Articles 14, equality before law, and 21, protection of life and personal liberty, do apply to every person, including foreign nationals.

Kaushal identified the greater risk as immigration consequences rather than protest law itself. Under Section 7D of the Citizenship Act, 1955, OCI registration can be cancelled on specified grounds, including breaking Indian law or acting against public interest or security, after a hearing. Separately, the Centre holds wide powers to ask a foreign national to leave.

At the protest itself, Khan had described himself as a city resident concerned about restrictions on movement and voices being suppressed, saying he had no specific demands and was not part of any organisation.

What this means for OCI holders

For the millions of diaspora members who live in India on OCI status, the practical lesson is specific. Your card secures long-term residence and work, but it does not convert a political act into a citizen's protected act. Joining a political protest can be treated as an immigration issue, with consequences up to a leave-India direction and, separately, possible OCI cancellation proceedings after a hearing. Anyone served such a notice should seek immigration counsel immediately and note the deadline in Khan's case: October 28.
